clue.text: Glum, the (eventual) result of not spitting feathers?

definitions.meaning: glum means miserable, low in spirits

definitions.text: the (eventual) result of not spitting feathers?
definitions.meaning: feathers are down; any you fail to spit out will eventually end up in the sewage dumps

explanation.surface: Someone muses on what happens if you don't spit out the feathers you've swallowed, and why it leaves you glum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spitting feathers' is British slang for being very thirsty or furious, which hides the literal reading: swallowed down travels on to the dumps.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a depressed, miserable mood, a standard synonym for feeling glum.

clue.text: Plain clothes police essentially ignorant

indicators.note: used as a verb: the first word dresses, so wraps round, the letters that follow

parts.note: plain, as in clear to see, means obvious

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so its central letters are taken

explanation.surface: A report that plain-clothes police are basically clueless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain clothes' reads as one phrase, but 'clothes' is a verb meaning wraps round, and 'essentially' takes the heart of 'police'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being oblivious means being unaware of something, much as ignorant means lacking knowledge of it.

clue.text: Blatantly regressive concealing of birth

indicators.note: going back, so the concealed letters are read from right to left
the word Blatantly holds the needed letters inside it

explanation.surface: A complaint about a backward society blatantly hiding facts about births.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing' picks out LATAN inside 'Blatantly', and 'regressive' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: Natal is the adjective relating to the moment or place someone was born, as in natal day.

clue.text: Group of people of high rank? No thanks

definitions.text: Group of people of high rank?
definitions.note: a noblesse is a nobility, a group; the answer is its plural form

parts.note: to bless is to thank, as in blessing God for food, so thanks gives blesses

explanation.surface: Someone politely declines an invitation to join the aristocracy.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is loose: a noblesse is a nobility, and the answer is its plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Noblesse is the nobility, the class of aristocrats holding hereditary titles above commoners.

clue.text: Coffee seller changing taps for Lily

indicators.note: taps are marked C and H for cold and hot, so one tap letter is swapped for the other

parts.note: Costa is a big British chain of coffee shops

explanation.surface: A café chain swaps its plumbing to please someone called Lily.
explanation.walkthrough: COSTA is a UK coffee-shop chain. Bathroom taps are labelled C (cold) and H (hot), so its C becomes H.
explanation.definitionFit: The hosta is a shade-loving garden plant also known as the plantain lily.

clue.text: Solemn music from dreary Cambridgeshire town

parts.note: a dead place or party is dull and dreary
March is a market town in the Fens of Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: Mournful music said to come from a dull town in eastern England.
explanation.walkthrough: MARCH is a small town in the Cambridgeshire Fens.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead march is a slow funeral piece played as a procession escorts the coffin.

clue.text: Eccles getting help upon rejection in the papers, perhaps

parts.note: Eccles is the setter of this puzzle, who would refer to himself as me

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the word for help is turned round

parts.note: to aid is to help

explanation.surface: The setter, having asked for help and been turned down, ends up in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often refer to themselves by their pen-name, so Eccles gives ME; 'upon rejection' turns AID into DIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Newspapers are one example of the media, the channels of mass communication, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Australian longs for progress

definitions.meaning: longs are long trousers, and ... is Australian slang for trousers
to make ... is to make progress

explanation.surface: An Aussie yearning to get ahead in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'longs' looks like a verb, as in yearns, but it is a noun: long trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Trousers are called strides in Australian slang; strides also means advances or progress made.

clue.text: Threads about plugging Boris Johnson's statements?

indicators.note: a plug is pushed into a hole, so the short word is stuck inside the longer one

parts.note: a wry jibe: the former UK prime minister was notorious for fibs, small lies
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A satirical jab at the truthfulness of a former British prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the jibe at Boris Johnson, the former UK prime minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Fibres are fine strands of material, the same as threads.

clue.text: Small piece of land in narrow strip of water, north to south

indicators.note: N, north, is turned into S, south

parts.note: an inlet is a narrow arm of sea running into land

explanation.surface: Geographic directions for finding a small island in a channel running from north to south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'north to south' reads as a direction of travel, but it swaps N for S in INLET.
explanation.definitionFit: An islet is a very small island, a tiny piece of land surrounded by water.

clue.text: Spectator and Times support the Queen

parts.note: by means times in multiplication, as in two by three
a stand holds something up, so supports it
ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Two newspapers, The Spectator and The Times, backing the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The Spectator and The Times are British publications; here only the first is the definition, and 'Times' gives BY.
explanation.definitionFit: A bystander is a person present at an event who watches without taking part, an onlooker.

clue.text: Ponder rejecting big fan of Enigmatic Variations' introductions

indicators.note: rejecting means sending back, so the phrase is read backwards
the introduction of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: a lover of something is a big fan of it

explanation.surface: Musing on spurning someone devoted to Elgar's famous orchestral work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejecting' reverses EV LOVER, the initials of 'Enigmatic Variations' followed by their lover, giving REVOL then VE.
explanation.definitionFit: To revolve an idea is to turn it over in the mind, so to ponder it.

clue.text: A group of Marines that helps you stay afloat?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun, the inflatable band a learner swimmer wears

parts.note: RM is the abbreviation for the Royal Marines
a band is a group, of musicians or people

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a unit of commandos could keep you from sinking.
explanation.walkthrough: RM stands for the Royal Marines, the British naval infantry.
explanation.definitionFit: An armband here is an inflatable ring worn on the upper arm by children learning to swim.

clue.text: Keep quiet about husband of salty individual showing laziness

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word surrounds the second

parts.note: sh is the command to keep quiet
in Genesis, Lot's wife was turned into a pillar of salt

explanation.surface: Someone keeps mum about a man whose wife was salty, which seems idle.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'salty individual' is Lot's wife in Genesis, who became a pillar of salt; her husband is LOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Sloth is the habit of idleness, one of the seven deadly sins, so a synonym of laziness.

clue.text: Ethanol is abused in a bit of cold weather

indicators.note: abused means mistreated, so these letters are knocked into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Drinking alcohol on a chilly day goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abused' is the anagram signal on ETHANOLIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A hailstone is a single pellet of ice falling in a storm, a small piece of wintry weather.

clue.text: Most of planet worried by Sweden's floods

indicators.note: most of a word is all but its final letter

parts.note: Saturn is the ringed planet
ate, as in 'what's eating you?', means worried
S is the international vehicle code for Sweden

explanation.surface: A huge planet anxious about Swedish floodwaters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most of' removes the N at the end of SATURN; ATE means worried, as in something eating at you.
explanation.definitionFit: To saturate something is to soak it completely, so saturates means floods or drenches.

clue.text: Ability to withstand hardship shown by European scratching head in daze

indicators.note: in places the shortened word inside the word for a daze

parts.note: a trance is a dazed state

indicators.note: scratching out the head of a word deletes its first letter

parts.note: a Pole is a European, from Poland

explanation.surface: A dazed European scratches his head yet keeps calm under strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scratching head' removes the P from POLE; the OLE left is put 'in' TRANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance is the capacity to endure pain or difficulty without giving in.

clue.text: I cut arm at training, which is distressing

indicators.note: training reshapes something, so these letters are put through their paces into a new order

explanation.surface: An athlete cuts their arm during a training session, a nasty experience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'training' is the anagram signal on ICUTARMAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something traumatic causes deep shock or upset, which is what distressing means.

clue.text: Is son restricted by awful rejection?

indicators.note: being restricted by something means being hemmed in by it, so the first pieces sit inside

parts.note: dismal means awful, dreadful
s is the abbreviation for son, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Asking whether a boy is held back by a cruel rebuff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' is not a link word here but part of the wordplay; 'restricted by' means held inside the word for awful.
explanation.definitionFit: A dismissal is the act of sending someone away or turning down an idea, a rejection.

clue.text: I'd party with abandon in short excursion

indicators.note: abandon means wildness, so these letters are thrown about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone declares they'd party wildly on a brief outing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with abandon' is the anagram signal on IDPARTY.
explanation.definitionFit: A day trip is an outing there and back within one day, so a brief journey.

clue.text: Has once pinched the backside of Little Ted?

indicators.note: pinched means squeezed between, so the archaic word clasps the letter

parts.note: hath is the old form of has

indicators.note: the backside is the rear, so the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about whether someone once pinched a small child's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little Ted' looks like a nickname, but 'Little' gives E and 'Ted?' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ted Heath, Edward Heath, was British Conservative prime minister 1970 to 1974; the question mark marks the example.

clue.text: Poor country abandoned by Austria

indicators.note: abandoned by means left without, so a letter is dropped

parts.note: Hungary is a central European country
A is the international vehicle code for Austria

explanation.surface: A struggling nation deserted by its neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: A is Austria's international vehicle code; dropping it from HUNGARY leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Hungry soil is poor, barren land, a dictionary sense alongside wanting food.

clue.text: Source of nutrition you nearly left by overturned barrel

indicators.note: nearly means not quite, so the last letter goes
an overturned thing is upside down, so in a down light, read backwards

parts.note: a cask is a barrel

explanation.surface: Someone tells you a food supply was almost left beside a toppled barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nearly' trims YOU to YO; 'overturned' reverses CASK to KSAC.
explanation.definitionFit: The yolk sac is the membrane holding the yolk that feeds a developing embryo.

clue.text: Drunk on just under two pints

parts.note: lit is slang for drunk
re, on the subject of, means on

explanation.surface: Getting drunk on a little less than two pints of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' is not a link: RE means concerning, as 'on' does in 'a talk on birds'.
explanation.definitionFit: A litre is about 1.76 imperial pints, so a little less than two.

clue.text: Greek characters leaving French wine for trainee

indicators.note: the Greek letters leave, so they are taken out of the wine

parts.note: Muscadet is a dry white wine from the Loire valley
mus is the plural of mu, a Greek letter

explanation.surface: Some Greeks walk out on a French white, leaving a learner behind.
explanation.walkthrough: MUS is the plural of the Greek letter mu.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a young person training for the armed forces or police, so a trainee.

clue.text: Course of treatment, say, taken by miner in a bad way

indicators.note: taken in by the shuffled word, so the short piece sits inside it
being in a bad way means in poor shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: eg, for example, means say

explanation.surface: A treatment plan for a miner in poor health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a bad way' rearranges the miner's letters as RIMEN, and 'taken by' sets the example abbreviation after its R.
explanation.definitionFit: A regimen is a prescribed programme of diet, exercise or medicine, a course of treatment.

clue.text: Mess up foxtrot turn

parts.note: to goof is to blunder or mess up
Foxtrot is the radio code word for F

explanation.surface: A ballroom dancer botches a turn in the foxtrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foxtrot' is not the dance but the radio alphabet's F.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk that turns goes sour; to go off means the same, to spoil.

clue.text: Backwards-looking study describing duke gone over again

parts.note: retro styles look back to the past

indicators.note: describing a circle means drawing round it, so the word for study goes round

parts.note: a den is a study, a private room

explanation.surface: A nostalgic study that writes about a duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' means drawing round, so DEN goes round D.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrodden is the past participle of retread, so walked over again.

clue.text: Swimmer staggers as if drunk when taking clothes off

indicators.note: stripping off clothes removes the outer layer, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: to totter is to walk unsteadily, like a drunk

explanation.surface: A tipsy bather wobbles while undressing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking clothes off' strips the outer T and S from TOTTERS.
explanation.definitionFit: The otter is an aquatic mammal and an expert swimmer, an example of the class.

clue.text: Broadcast for every boring responsible student becoming tense

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the first pieces go inside the word for student

parts.note: a prefect is a senior pupil given duties in a British school
sent means transmitted, as a broadcast is
per means for each or every

explanation.surface: A senior pupil, trusted with duties, grows nervous on air.
explanation.walkthrough: A prefect is a senior pupil with disciplinary duties in a British school. 'boring' drills the other pieces into it after its third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The present perfect is a verb tense, as in 'I have eaten', joining past action to now.
